Baltimore’s Abandoned Homes Are Now in High Demand
 
Plus, Jeff Bezos and Jared Kushner can’t get into this exclusive Miami country club
 
By Craig Karmin
 

This is an edition of the Real Estate newsletter, a weekly briefing of the biggest commercial deals, news, analysis and trends in office, multifamily, retail and other commercial sectors. If you’re not subscribed, sign up here.

 


People like Chris Waldron, a plumber and part-time property investor, are the face of Baltimore’s housing recovery. He recently paid $45,000 for one of the city’s vacant homes, with boarded up windows and a peeling facade. His plan is to spend $130,000 to fix up the property and then resell it for over $300,000. Thanks to investors like Waldron, Baltimore has cut the number of vacant homes by nearly a third over the last decade and it has jump-started plans to eliminate the problem entirely by 2038. Nicholas G. Miller explains why Baltimore is ahead of other American cities that have attempted similar strategies to reduce blight.

 

Seemingly every billionaire moving to Miami wants to join the Indian Creek Country Club, the city’s nearly century-old exclusive membership club. Owning a property on Indian Creek island doesn’t guarantee admission to the country club, which features a private golf course, a clubhouse modeled on a Mediterranean villa, and a swimming pool with bayfront views of the Miami skyline. Some of the island’s more recent residents include Jared Kushner and Ivanka Trump, Bezos, the Qatari royal family, and Mark Zuckerberg. None of them are members of the club. Deborah Acosta reports on who gets in and why.

 
 
 

Abandoned Homes in Baltimore Are Now Being Fought Over in Bidding Wars

 
 
KT KANAZAWICH FOR WSJ
 

With its boarded-up windows and peeling facade, the vacant building didn’t seem like the kind of house that would prompt a bidding war. But after competitors doubled what he had wanted to pay, Chris Waldron, a plumber and part-time property investor, reluctantly raised his auction card to offer $45,000 for the chance to fix up and then resell the property.

 

The purchase is part of one of the most improbable reversals in Baltimore’s history and for any of America’s beleaguered housing markets: Thousands of Baltimore vacant homes, which for decades dragged down neighborhoods and repelled investment, are now in demand.

 
 
 
$235,333
 

Baltimore’s median home price, according to Zillow. That is much lower than the national median of $381,333.

The Rich and Famous Who Can’t Get Into Miami’s Most Exclusive Country Club

 
 
ANTHONY DEVLIN/GETTY IMAGES
 

Jeff Bezos and his wife Lauren Sánchez Bezos were special guests in February for the annual dock party at Indian Creek Country Club, where members gathered to meet the famed entrepreneur. He went to the event hoping to persuade board members to admit him to the club, according to people who attended the event. Six months later, Bezos still hasn’t received an invitation to join the club.

Indian Creek represents one of South Florida’s major battlefields where the region’s newly minted billionaires are clashing with those of more modest affluence who often trace their Miami roots back generations.

 
 
 
$234 Million
 

The amount Jeff Bezos has spent to acquire three properties on Indian Creek island, according to public records.

 
 
 

Data Points

 

• 35%: The portion of home builders who cut prices in August, down 2 percentage points from the month before, according to the latest National Association of Home Builders/Wells Fargo Housing Market Index.

 

• 2.3%: The decrease in pending home sales in July compared with the month before, according to the National Association of Realtors. It was the lowest level since January.

 

• 13,300: The number of Phoenix apartments that were absorbed in the first half of this year, a 68% jump from the same period last year as the city works through a historic supply glut, according to CoStar.
